steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s an overview of the key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar Component  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose sugar (lacking an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA contains ribose sugar (with a hydroxyl, –OH, at the 2′ carbon).  

2. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and uracil (U) instead of thymine.  

3. Strand Structure  
   • DNA is usually double-stranded, forming a stable double helix held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A–T and G–C).  
   • RNA is typically single-stranded and can fold into complex three-dimensional shapes via intramolecular base pairing.  

4. Location in the Cell  
   • DNA resides mainly in the cell nucleus (in eukaryotes) and in small amounts in mitochondria and chloroplasts. In prokaryotes, DNA is in the nucleoid region.  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (eukaryotes) and then travels to the cytoplasm; in prokaryotes, it’s made and functions in the cytoplasm.  

5. Function  
   • DNA stores and transmits the genetic blueprint for all cellular structures and functions across generations.  
   • RNA performs several roles, chiefly in decoding that blueprint and carrying out its instructions:  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes.  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA): brings amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis.  
     – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): a structural and catalytic component of ribosomes.  
     – Other RNAs (e.g., microRNA, siRNA, long noncoding RNA) regulate gene expression and RNA processing.  

6. Stability and Lifespan  
   • DNA is chemically more stable (the missing 2′-OH makes it less prone to hydrolysis), allowing it to serve as a long-term information store.  
   • RNA, with its extra 2′-OH, is more reactive and generally has a shorter cellular half-life—appropriate for molecules whose levels must rapidly change.  

7. Replication vs. Transcription  
   • DNA replication: makes an identical copy of the DNA double helix, catalyzed by DNA polymerases, before cell division.  
   • Transcription: uses one strand of DNA as a template to synthesize RNA, catalyzed by RNA polymerases; only specific genes are transcribed as needed.  

8. Modifications  
   • DNA can be chemically modified (e.g., cytosine methylation) to regulate gene expression epigenetically.  
   • RNA undergoes extensive post-transcriptional modifications (capping, polyadenylation, splicing in eukaryotes; base modifications in tRNA/rRNA) that affect its stability, localization, and function.  

Summary  
  – DNA is a stable, double-stranded, deoxyribose-based molecule that stores hereditary information.  
  – RNA is a more transient, single-stranded, ribose-based molecule that carries out and regulates the expression of that information.
